extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and general readers seeking criteria for evaluating or creating morally and socially effective art
extracted.subtask_description: A prescriptive framework for judging works of art by whether they transmit feelings that unite people and align with the dominant 'religious perception' (in the author's sense) of the age — especially brotherhood and love — and for distinguishing universal/good art from exclusive/counterfeit art. Useful for critics, writers, and artists deciding what art to encourage or reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of art — transmission of feeling (infection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art's purpose is the transmission of feeling: 'Art remains ... nothing but the infection by one man of another ... with the feelings experienced by the infector.' The better art more fully fulfils this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First test a work by whether it genuinely transmits the artist's feeling to others (is 'infectious'). If it fails to infect, it may be a counterfeit. Examples/notes: infectiousness can be limited (infects a small class) or wide (infects all); infectiousness is the first threshold before finer moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of appraisal — the religious perception of the age
rubrics_metrics.description: The feelings transmitted by art must be estimated by the religious perception of the given time and society; that perception indicates what feelings are 'good' or 'necessary for the well-being of mankind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the prevailing 'religious perception' (broad life-conception) of the age as the normative yardstick. The author stresses that even secular attacks on religion presuppose an underlying religious perception by which they judge life and art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern religious perception — brotherhood and loving harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: For the author's (modern/Christian) age the central religious perception is that human well-being lies in the growth of brotherhood and loving harmony among all men; art should be appraised on this basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work promotes 'union of all men' and brotherly love (material and spiritual well-being through union). Works that foster love, self-sacrifice, pity, devotion, and respect for others align with this perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should unite, not divide
rubrics_metrics.description: Good art evokes feelings that unite people in soul and sympathy; bad art evokes exclusive feelings that separate groups and create enmity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject art whose subject-matter or feeling is essentially divisive (patriotic exclusivity, cult-specific devotion, aristocratic snobbery). Example anti-patterns: patriotic anthems, sectarian cult art, art celebrating social superiority—these are classed as 'bad' because they divide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / accessibility of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Good art transmits feelings accessible to all men without exception (not only to a particular class, nationality, education level or cult). Universal accessibility is a central criterion of good subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a peasant, a child, an old man, or someone of another nation could apprehend and share the feelings produced. Examples of universal works: the biblical story of Joseph; simple melodies and folk-like ornamentation; certain Dickens stories (as cited) that reach wide audiences. Anti-pattern: art overloaded with local detail or specialised reference that restricts comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of good art — religious and universal
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two legitimate categories of good art in the age described: (1) religious art transmitting feelings flowing from a religious perception (love of God and neighbour, and indignation at violation of love), and (2) universal art transmitting the simplest common-life feelings accessible to everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this typology to classify works: religious art often appears chiefly in words (and some painting/sculpture); universal art can appear in all forms but especially music, painting, and everyday ornamentation. Both aim to unite people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content criterion over formal beauty or technical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal beauty, technical virtuosity, or elaborate technique alone do not make good art; the decisive factor is whether the work transmits the appropriate unifying feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of works that emphasize 'technique and the beauty of the picture' at the expense of infectious feeling—these can be misleadingly praised while failing the moral/unity test. Example: Gérôme’s 'Pollice Verso' admired for spectacle rather than horror; celebrated painters' Gospel scenes that depict events but cannot transmit religious feeling if the artist lacks it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and restraint promote universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Superfluous detail and excessive local colouring hinder the transmission of universal feelings; restraint leaves only essential elements that can be apprehended by all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating narrative or visual art, ask whether removing nonessential details would leave a story/picture that still transmits the feeling. The biblical Joseph story is held up as a model of necessary restraint. Anti-pattern: 'realism' or provincialism that piles on detail and becomes less universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject 'exclusive' subject-matter (aristocratic, sensual, elitist feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter devoted to aristocratic honour, satiety, spleen, refined cynical sexuality, or other class-bound/exclusive feelings is bad art because it is incomprehensible and non-unifying for the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify works portraying idle rich amusements, voluptuous subjects (female nudity for its own sake), or elite affectations as harmful/counterfeit art. Examples cited: much chamber and opera music and upper-class literary fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music-specific criterion — melodic freedom and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody should be free and understandable by all; complex harmonic/rhythmic/orchestral complications that require specialized training make music exclusive and therefore bad as universal art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate music by whether ordinary people can grasp and be moved by the melody without specialized harmonic training. Anti-patterns: piling complex modulations onto trivial melodies (national/exclusive harmonic schools), long confusing works whose effect is incomprehensible to the general crowd (the author's critique of Beethoven's Ninth). Examples of acceptable bits: certain arias/nocturnes and simple folk-like melodies; marches and dances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentation and 'low' arts count if they transmit feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects commonly dismissed as mere ornament (china dolls, patterns, landscapes, genre pictures) qualify as good art if they transmit a true feeling comprehensible to everyone—the criterion is feeling, not abstract 'beauty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss decorative or folk arts on grounds of low status; evaluate them by whether they evoke common admiration or delight accessible to all. The author argues these often are more universally communicative than pretentious haute art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage evaluation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine if a production is real art (i.e., infectious to someone). Second, determine whether it is exclusive (bad in subject-matter) or uniting (good), and if good, whether it is religious art (transmitting love to God/neighbor) or universal art (transmitting simple common-life feelings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rubric gives an algorithmic approach: (1) infectiousness → (2) accessibility/unity test → (3) subtype classification. Use concrete examples (Beethoven’s Ninth judged non-infectious to the general public; thus excluded as good universal art) to calibrate judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge examples by the unified-feeling test, not reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation, fame, or historical exaltation do not override the criterion that a work must unite people by transmitting appropriate feelings; many celebrated works may fail the test and should be re-evaluated accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same tests even to canonical works (Divine Comedy, parts of Shakespeare and Goethe, Raphael’s religious paintings). The author insists on reason and common-sense criteria rather than deference to established prestige.
